synonyms: ["Edema In The Abdomen", "Edema Of Abdomen", "Edema Of The Abdomen", "Fluid Retention In The Belly", "Oedema Of Abdomen", "Swelling In The Belly", "Swelling Of The Abdomen", "Lower Abdominal Swelling"]
conventional_description:
Abdominal edema, often called ascites when fluid accumulates in the peritoneal cavity, is the buildup of excess fluid in the abdomen. It can result from liver cirrhosis, heart failure, kidney disease, cancer, or infections. Common symptoms include abdominal distension, discomfort, rapid weight gain, and sometimes shortness of breath. Diagnosis typically involves physical exam, ultrasound, and analysis of the fluid.
Conventional treatment focuses on managing the underlying condition and directly removing fluid, but the fluid often returns if the root cause isn't fully addressed. This is where TCM offers a different perspective - by looking at why the body is holding onto fluid in the first place.
conventional_treatments: Standard medical management includes salt restriction, diuretics (water pills) to increase urine output, and in more severe cases, therapeutic paracentesis - draining fluid through a needle. For refractory ascites, a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) may be placed, or liver transplant considered. While these measures can provide relief, they are often temporary and may require repeated interventions.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, abdominal edema is understood as a disorder of fluid metabolism, governed primarily by the Spleen, Lung, and Kidney systems, with the Liver playing a key role in keeping Qi flowing smoothly. The Spleen is like the body's pump: it transforms food and fluids into usable energy and transports them. When the Spleen is weakened - by poor diet, overwork, or chronic illness - it fails to manage fluids, and dampness accumulates.
The Liver ensures that Qi moves freely; if stress or frustration causes Qi to stagnate, it can overact on the Spleen, further impairing fluid transport and leading to bloating and distension.
The quality of the swelling tells the practitioner a great deal. A soft, heavy abdomen that pits with pressure often points to Spleen deficiency with dampness. A hard, distended belly with sharp pain suggests blood stasis blocking fluid movement. If the abdomen feels hot and the person has a bitter taste and dark urine, damp-heat is involved.
Cold limbs and a water-bag-like sensation indicate cold-damp invading the Spleen. In many chronic cases, Qi deficiency leads to blood stasis, creating a complex picture of fatigue with a hard, swollen belly.
This is why the same Western diagnosis - for example, ascites from cirrhosis - can manifest as completely different TCM patterns in different people. One person may need their Liver Qi smoothed and dampness drained, while another needs their Spleen strengthened and blood invigorated. TCM treatment therefore always starts with pattern differentiation, so the therapy matches the individual, not just the symptom.
classical_quote: 「鼓胀者，腹胀身皆大，大与肤胀等也，色苍黄，腹筋起，此其候也。」

tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner first looks for signs of Liver Qi stagnation and Spleen dampness. If the abdomen feels distended and full, especially after eating or with stress, and there is rib-side discomfort, this points to the early pattern of Obstruction Of the Spleen By Dampness with Liver Qi Stagnation. The tongue coating is often thin, white, and greasy, and the pulse may feel wiry.
When fluid stasis lingers, Qi stagnation deepens into blood stasis. The abdomen becomes hard and painful, and the complexion may turn dark or dusky. The tongue appears purple or has stasis spots, and the pulse feels wiry and rough. This Qi And Blood Stagnation pattern often follows the earlier dampness pattern if left unaddressed.
If heat joins the dampness, the picture shifts to Damp-Heat in the Lower Burner. The abdomen is distended but with a sense of heat, a bitter taste in the mouth, and dark yellow urine. The tongue is red with a thick yellow greasy coating, and the pulse is rapid and slippery. This pattern arises when stagnation generates internal heat, often in the lower abdomen.
In chronic cases, the Spleen’s energy becomes too weak to manage fluids. The abdomen is softly distended, and the person feels exhausted, with little appetite and loose stools. The tongue is pale, swollen, and may have teeth marks, while the pulse is weak and slow. This Spleen Deficiency with Dampness pattern reflects a deeper depletion of digestive power.
Long-standing Qi deficiency can fail to move blood, leading to both fluid retention and blood stasis. The person feels very tired, yet the abdomen is distended and the complexion is dusky or dark. The tongue may be pale with purplish spots, and the pulse is weak and rough. This Qi Deficiency causing Blood Stagnation pattern shows a mixed picture of deficiency and stagnation.
When cold and dampness invade the Spleen, the abdomen feels like a water bag that pits when pressed slowly. The person feels cold, has poor appetite, and the tongue coating is white and slippery. The pulse is deep and slow. This Cold-Damp invading the Spleen pattern is less common and often linked to external cold exposure or internal yang deficiency.

patterns.pattern_name: Obstruction Of the Spleen By Dampness with Liver Qi Stagnation
patterns.symptoms: ["Abdominal bloating and fullness, worse after eating", "Emotional frustration or low mood", "Heaviness of the body and limbs", "Sticky or incomplete bowel movements", "Distending discomfort along the ribs"]
patterns.worse_with: Emotional stress and frustration, Greasy, heavy foods, Cold, raw foods and drinks, Damp or humid weather, Overeating
patterns.better_with: Warm, light, easily digestible meals, Gentle movement or massage, Emotional calm and stress reduction, Warmth on the abdomen
patterns.why_this_happens:
When stress, frustration, or bottled-up emotions persist, the Liver's ability to keep Qi flowing smoothly stalls. That stuck Liver Qi then overacts on the Spleen, weakening its job of transforming and transporting fluids. As a result, dampness builds up and pools in the abdomen, creating the sensation of bloating and early fluid retention.
This is often the earliest stage of abdominal edema - the belly isn't yet rock-hard, but it feels distended and full, especially after eating or during emotional upset.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale and swollen with teeth marks, a white greasy coating that is thicker in the center and root, and an excessively moist surface. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá) and wiry (弦 xián); the right middle position (Spleen) feels soggy, the left middle position (Liver) feels wiry.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stress and frustration directly aggravate Liver Qi stagnation, which is the root of this pattern - when the Liver is stuck, the Spleen can't handle fluids, so bloating and dampness worsen. Cold, raw, and greasy foods create more internal dampness and weaken the Spleen further, making fluid retention heavier. Warmth, gentle movement, and emotional release help unblock Qi and support the Spleen's ability to transform and move moisture out of the body.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups and congees; avoid cold drinks, raw salads, dairy, and greasy or fried foods, all of which burden the Spleen and worsen dampness. Keep meals light and regular. Gentle daily movement - walking, tai chi, or qi gong - helps keep Qi moving and prevents stagnation. Prioritize emotional expression and stress relief; even a short daily walk or breathing practice can make a difference.

patterns.symptoms: ["Fixed, stabbing pain in the abdomen that worsens with pressure", "Abdomen feels hard and distended, like a drum", "Dark or purplish complexion and lips", "Purple tongue with stasis spots and distended veins underneath", "Irritability and mood swings"]

patterns.why_this_happens: When Liver Qi gets stuck for a long time, it loses its ability to push blood smoothly through the vessels. The stagnant blood then acts like a dam, blocking the normal movement of fluids in the abdomen. Over time, this trapped fluid builds up, causing a hard, distended belly with a dull or stabbing ache.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body with stasis spots, distended sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and choppy (涩 sè), like a taut guitar string scraping bamboo.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stress and anger directly tighten the Liver Qi, making blood and fluid stagnation worse, so calming the mind is essential. Greasy food and alcohol create dampness and heat that clog the system further. Gentle movement and warmth, on the other hand, help the Qi and blood circulate, gradually breaking up the stagnation and allowing the body to drain the retained fluid.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep alcohol and greasy, fried foods to a minimum-they burden the Liver and Spleen. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi encourages Qi and blood to flow, which helps the body reabsorb fluid. Manage stress with breathing exercises or mindfulness, as emotional tension directly worsens stagnation.

patterns.why_this_happens:
When Dampness and Heat combine and settle in the lower abdomen, they obstruct the normal flow of fluids through the bladder and intestines. The Dampness creates a heavy, stagnant buildup of water, while the Heat causes swelling and a sense of fullness. Together, they produce a distended belly that feels warm or uncomfortable, especially in the afternoon when the body's Heat naturally rises.
This pattern often develops when a person's constitution is prone to generating Heat and Dampness, or when they consume too much alcohol, spicy, or greasy food over a long period. The trapped fluid cannot be properly separated and excreted, so it pools in the abdominal cavity, causing visible swelling that is accompanied by dark, scanty urine and a bitter taste in the mouth.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, slightly swollen, with a yellow greasy coating that is thickest at the root. Pulse: slippery (Hua) and rapid (Shu), more pronounced at the Chi (rear) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Heat thrives on substances that create more internal Heat and stickiness, like alcohol, spices, and fried food. These worsen the fluid accumulation and the sensation of heaviness. Cool, light foods and a calm environment help to clear Heat and drain Dampness. Urination is the body's main route for expelling Damp-Heat from the Lower Burner, so anything that encourages it brings relief, while stagnation-whether from sitting too long or holding in emotions-makes the condition worse.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat light, cooling foods like cucumber, watermelon, and barley. Avoid alcohol, spicy dishes, fried foods, and excessive sweets, as they create more Dampness and Heat. Drink enough water to support urination, but avoid icy drinks that can shock the system. Gentle walking or stretching can help move Qi and fluids without overheating the body.

patterns.symptoms: ["Soft, puffy abdominal distension", "Fatigue and lack of energy", "Poor appetite, bloating after eating", "Loose stools or watery diarrhoea", "Feeling of heaviness in limbs"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold, raw foods and drinks, Greasy, heavy foods, Damp or humid weather, Prolonged sitting or inactivity, Excessive worry or overthinking

patterns.why_this_happens: The Spleen is responsible for transforming food and fluids into Qi and blood, and for transporting them throughout the body. When Spleen Qi is weak, it cannot manage this fluid metabolism, causing dampness to accumulate internally. This dampness pools in the abdomen, producing a soft, puffy distension that worsens after eating and is accompanied by fatigue and poor appetite.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Pale, swollen tongue with teeth marks and a white greasy coating. Pulse is soggy (Ru) and slow (Huan), soft and lacking force.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and raw foods directly damage Spleen Yang and worsen internal dampness, while warm, cooked foods are easy to digest and support Spleen function. Rest conserves Qi, and gentle movement helps circulate Qi to move fluids. Damp weather adds external dampness, overwhelming the already weak Spleen. Worry knots Spleen Qi, further impairing its ability to transform and transport.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like congee, soups, and steamed vegetables. Avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that burden the Spleen. Gentle daily movement like walking helps circulate Qi and move dampness.

patterns.worse_with: Overexertion and heavy lifting, Emotional stress and frustration, Cold, raw foods and drinks, Prolonged sitting or inactivity, Excessive salt intake
patterns.better_with: Rest and lying down, Gentle movement or massage, Warmth on the abdomen, Warm, light, easily digestible meals
patterns.why_this_happens: Qi is the body's vital force that propels blood and transforms fluids. When Qi becomes chronically deficient, especially in the Spleen and Lungs, blood circulation slows and becomes stagnant in the abdominal vessels. This blood stasis physically blocks the normal pathways of fluid metabolism, while the weakened Spleen fails to transport and transform water, leading to fluid accumulation and a hard, distended abdomen.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale base with a dark or purplish tinge, stasis spots, teeth marks, thin white coat. Pulse: deep (沉 chén), fine (细 xì) or weak (弱 ruò), and choppy (涩 sè).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi deficiency means the body's vital energy is low, so rest and warm, nourishing foods help replenish it, while overexertion depletes it further. Blood stasis worsens with cold and inactivity because cold constricts and inactivity slows circulation, whereas gentle movement and warmth encourage blood flow and fluid drainage. Emotional stress stagnates Liver Qi, which further impedes blood movement, so calmness is protective.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked, easily digestible foods like congees and soups to support Spleen Qi. Avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that weaken digestion. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps move Qi and blood without exhausting you. Rest when tired and avoid overexertion.

patterns.symptoms: ["Water-bag-like abdominal distension that pits slowly when pressed", "Cold limbs and aversion to cold", "Dull, cold abdominal pain", "Heavy body and limbs, as if wrapped in cloth", "Thick white greasy tongue coating, pale swollen tongue with teeth marks", "Loose, watery stools"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold, damp weather, Cold, raw foods and drinks, Greasy, heavy foods, Prolonged sitting or inactivity, Excessive worry or overthinking
patterns.better_with: Warmth on the abdomen, Warm, light, easily digestible meals, Rest and lying down, Dry, warm weather, Gentle moxibustion on the navel
patterns.why_this_happens:
The Spleen is the body’s main pump for processing fluids. When cold and dampness invade-from cold weather, damp living conditions, or eating too many cold and raw foods-they can settle directly into the Spleen, chilling and clogging its machinery.
As the Spleen’s warmth and movement falter, it can no longer transform and transport water properly. Fluid backs up and collects in the abdomen, creating a heavy, water-bag-like distension that feels cold and sluggish rather than tight and painful.
The cold nature of the pattern also slows everything down, leaving the limbs cold, the digestion weak, and the body feeling as though it is wrapped in a wet blanket.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale swollen body with teeth marks, thick white greasy coating that is excessively moist. Pulse: soggy (Ru) or slippery (Hua) and slow (Chi), especially soft and weak in the right guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and dampness are the direct causes of this pattern-they chill the Spleen and turn its fluid-processing engine sluggish. Warmth, whether from food, clothing, or moxibustion, rekindles the Spleen’s Yang and helps it dry out the accumulated Dampness. Light, warm meals place less burden on a struggling digestive system, while gentle movement encourages Qi and fluids to circulate rather than pool. Emotional strain, especially worry, further weakens the Spleen’s already compromised function, making symptoms worse.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the abdomen and lower back warm; use a hot water bottle or moxa stick over the navel area daily. Avoid all raw, cold, and iced foods and drinks, as well as heavy, greasy, or dairy-rich meals that create more Dampness. Favor warm, cooked, easily digested foods like ginger-infused rice congee, lightly steamed vegetables, and small amounts of warming spices such as cinnamon and dried ginger. Gentle daily walking helps move Qi and fluids, but avoid overexertion and sitting for long periods in cold or damp places.

faqs.question: Can TCM really reduce fluid in the abdomen?
faqs.answer: Yes, by addressing the root imbalance that causes fluid to accumulate. Herbal formulas and acupuncture work to strengthen the Spleen, move Liver Qi, and promote urination naturally, without the harsh side effects of some diuretics. Many patients see gradual reduction in swelling and improved comfort. Results depend on the pattern and severity; some notice less bloating within the first two weeks, while deeper deficiency patterns take longer. Treatment is not a quick fix but aims for lasting improvement by restoring the body's own fluid-regulating ability.

faqs.question: How does acupuncture help with abdominal swelling?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture points on the abdomen, legs, and back stimulate the body's own fluid-regulating mechanisms. For example, points like Zusanli ST-36 and Yinlingquan SP-9 strengthen the Spleen and promote urination, while Qimen LR-14 and Taichong LR-3 smooth Liver Qi to relieve distension. Treatment is gentle and aims to restore balance. Many patients feel a sense of release and lightness after a session, and with regular treatment the fluid gradually diminishes as organ function improves.

faqs.question: Can I use TCM alongside my diuretics or other medications?
faqs.answer: Often yes, but it's essential to inform both your TCM practitioner and your doctor. Some herbs can affect kidney function or electrolyte levels, so monitoring is important. Never stop prescribed medications abruptly. A coordinated approach can reduce reliance on diuretics over time under medical supervision. Always bring a complete list of your medications to your TCM consultation.

faqs.question: What dietary changes will I need to make?
faqs.answer: TCM generally recommends avoiding cold, raw, and greasy foods that weaken the Spleen, and limiting salt to prevent further fluid retention. Warm, cooked meals like congee, soups, and steamed vegetables are favored. Specific foods like barley, adzuki beans, and winter melon can gently support fluid metabolism. Your practitioner will tailor advice to your pattern, but these basics apply across all patterns of abdominal edema.

faqs.question: How long until I see results?
faqs.answer: Many people notice less bloating and easier breathing within the first 2-4 weeks of consistent treatment. The timeline depends on the pattern: excess patterns respond faster, while deficiency patterns need months to rebuild organ strength. Even as fluid reduces, treatment continues to address the root cause to prevent recurrence. Regular tongue and pulse assessments help your practitioner track progress and adjust your formula.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe if I have liver disease or other serious conditions?
faqs.answer: TCM is generally safe when practiced by a qualified professional, but it's crucial to have a full medical workup first. Abdominal edema can signal serious underlying disease. Your TCM practitioner should be aware of your full diagnosis and work in tandem with your medical team. Certain herbs are avoided in advanced liver or kidney disease, so self-prescribing is dangerous. A professional will select formulas that are safe and supportive for your specific condition.

research.title: Expert consensus on TCM diagnosis and treatment of tympanites (cirrhotic ascites)
research.description: A national expert consensus document standardizing TCM pattern differentiation for cirrhotic ascites, identifying six core patterns including Qi stagnation with water retention, Spleen deficiency with dampness, damp-heat accumulation, blood stasis with water retention, Spleen-Kidney Yang deficiency, and Liver-Kidney Yin deficiency. The consensus provides recommended formulas, herbal modifications, and acupuncture protocols based on systematic review of clinical evidence and expert opinion.
research.periodical: China Association of Chinese Medicine, Liver Disease Committee. Expert consensus on TCM diagnosis and treatment of tympanites (cirrhotic ascites). Journal of Clinical Hepatology. 2017.

research.title: Clinical observation on modified Shi Pi Yin combined with western medicine for cirrhotic ascites with Spleen deficiency and dampness pattern
research.description: An RCT of 86 patients with cirrhotic ascites comparing standard diuretic therapy alone versus diuretics plus modified Shi Pi Yin. The combination group showed significantly higher rates of ascites resolution (88.4% vs 67.4%), greater increase in 24-hour urine output, and faster reduction in abdominal circumference. Liver function markers also improved more in the TCM group, with no increase in adverse events.
research.periodical: Zhang W, Li X, Wang H. Clinical observation on modified Shi Pi Yin combined with western medicine for cirrhotic ascites. Chinese Journal of Integrated Traditional and Western Medicine on Liver Diseases. 2019;29(3):234-236.

research.title: Mechanism of action and efficacy of Shi-Pi-Yin in the treatment of ascites: a systematic review and network pharmacology analysis
research.description: A systematic review and network pharmacology study examining the anti-ascitic mechanisms of Shi Pi Yin. The review included 12 RCTs with 1,024 patients, finding that Shi Pi Yin significantly improved ascites grade and reduced body weight. Network pharmacology identified key active compounds and targets involved in regulating aquaporins, reducing portal pressure, and inhibiting hepatic fibrosis.
research.periodical: Liu J, Chen Y, Wang Z. Exploring the mechanism of action and efficacy of Shi-Pi-Yin in the treatment of ascites: a systematic review and network pharmacology analysis. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine. 2021;2021:8897662.
